newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Doctors seen deciding date for Yeltsin surgery.
newsitem.headline: Doctors seen deciding date for Yeltsin surgery.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin's doctors were expected to meet on Monday to decide whether he was ready for a multiple bypass heart operation, but the Kremlin said no information would be available until later in the day.
A spokesman could neither confirm where the meeting, widely forecast in the Russian media, would take place nor when it would start.

But reporters noted tight security around the Cardiology Research Centre, where the operation is expected to be carried out. Sniffer dogs were active in the grounds of the building, in a western suburb of the Russian capital.

Pioneering U.S. heart surgery expert Michael DeBakey, who returned to Moscow on Sunday to attend the meeting and act as a consultant during the operation, has said the surgery was likely to go ahead early this week.
The Russian surgeons who will carry out the operation have said little about their plans and may not announce in advance when the 65-year-old president is to go under the knife.

A Kremlin spokesman said last week the doctors could decide when to operate "any day" but indicated that the first sign the operation was imminent could be an announcement that Yeltsin had temporarily handed over power to Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin.

Chernomyrdin has gradually taken on some of Yeltsin's duties in the four months since the president fell ill just before he was re-elected on July 3. The prime minister was due to chair a meeting of the influential Security Council starting at 3 p.m. (1200 GMT).

The council groups senior Russian ministers and security officials. It is normally chaired by the president. Itar-Tass news agency said Monday's meeting would discuss the situation in the breakaway republic of Chechnya.
Security Council officials Ivan Rybkin and Boris Berezovsky have both visited the rebel region.

The Kremlin has made clear that Yeltsin will sign a decree handing over full power to his understudy, giving him control of Russia's nuclear arsenal, only just before the surgery. A second decree hours later will annul it if all goes according to plan.
Yeltsin's wife Naina says her husband is optimistic and cracking jokes at the Barvikha sanatorium just outside Moscow where doctors have been giving him health tests.
"Of course he is worried, but he is outwardly calm. He has a good contact with his doctors. I hear humour and jokes," she said in a television interview.

Russian surgeon Renat Akchurin will lead the operation, which is expected to last six to eight hours. He and DeBakey said after the last full meeting of doctors on September 25 that the operation would be in the following six to 10 weeks.
Yeltsin is regarded by Western leaders as the main guarantor of stability in Moscow five years after the Soviet Union and communist rule collapsed.
The president, who has had at least two heart attacks, has been waiting since early September while doctors have treated him for anaemia, a thyroid problem and other ailments.
The surgery is needed to improve the supply of blood to his heart. DeBakey has said he can resume normal work within two months if the operation is successful.
